questions.question: What is an abstract class in Python?
questions.title: Abstract Classes with abc.ABC
questions.direct_answer: An abstract class defines a shared contract and may provide common behaviour, but cannot be instantiated while required abstract methods remain unimplemented. Python provides this mechanism through `abc.ABC` and `@abstractmethod`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can define a runtime-enforced family of classes with required operations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an abstract method cannot have any implementation or that the decorator alone works without `ABCMeta` through `ABC`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the instantiation boundary and show an abstract contract with useful concrete behaviour.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Inherit from `abc.ABC` to define an abstract base class conveniently.
A class with unresolved abstract methods cannot be instantiated.
Concrete subclasses must implement every required abstract member.
An abstract class may also contain normal shared methods and state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An abstract class represents a common contract for a related family of classes. In Python, it usually inherits from `ABC`, and methods that every concrete subclass must provide are marked with `@abstractmethod`.

The abstract-base-class machinery records those required members. Trying to instantiate a class while any remain abstract raises `TypeError`. Once a subclass implements all of them, it can be instantiated normally. The base may also provide constructors, helper methods, properties, and even a default body for an abstract method.

For example, a `PaymentMethod` ABC can require `pay(amount)`, while a concrete `CardPayment` implements the actual operation. A normal `validate_amount` method can stay in the base so every payment type shares one rule.

ABCs are valuable when the application owns a clear runtime family and incomplete implementations should fail early. They are not required for every polymorphic call; duck typing may be lighter when unrelated third-party objects only need to supply one operation. The abstraction should capture a stable contract, not force unrelated code into a deep hierarchy.

sections.title: Abstract contracts and concrete implementations
sections.content:
An abstraction names what clients may rely on while leaving implementation choices to concrete classes. The `abc` module gives that idea a runtime boundary. `ABC` uses `ABCMeta`, which tracks methods and properties marked abstract across the hierarchy.

A subclass is still abstract if even one required member has no concrete override. This catches an incomplete plugin or strategy when it is created rather than at the first missing method call. Shared base behaviour can reduce duplication, and an abstract method may contain cooperative logic that an override reaches with `super()`.

Runtime enforcement has a cost: implementations must join the nominal hierarchy. For internal strategy families that can be useful and explicit. For broad structural capabilities such as any object with `close()`, duck typing or a static `Protocol` may create less coupling. Abstraction is the design goal; an ABC is one tool for expressing it.

sections.title: From abstract contract to usable implementation
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[PaymentMethod ABC] --> R[Requires pay amount]
  A --> H[Provides validate_amount]
  C[CardPayment subclass] --> I[Implements pay]
  R --> C
  I --> O[Concrete class can be instantiated]
  R --> X[Missing implementation]
  X --> T[Instantiation raises TypeError]
```

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract base class and duck typing in Python?
questions.title: Abstract Base Class vs Duck Typing
questions.direct_answer: An abstract base class creates an explicit runtime-recognized contract and can block incomplete subclass instantiation. Duck typing accepts any object that provides the required behaviour, even when it has no shared base class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can choose between nominal runtime contracts and flexible structural behaviour.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Presenting one approach as always superior or confusing an ABC with a static `Protocol`.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose based on ownership, enforcement time, shared implementation, and third-party compatibility.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: An ABC defines an explicit nominal family and required members.
Incomplete regular subclasses of an ABC cannot be instantiated.
Duck typing checks usable behaviour when code performs an operation.
Unrelated and third-party types can work naturally through duck typing.
Use the least coupling that still makes the contract clear and safe.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An abstract base class is a nominal contract. Implementations normally inherit from the ABC, and Python can stop an incomplete subclass from being instantiated when abstract methods remain. The base can also supply shared code and supports checks such as `isinstance`.

Duck typing is structural at the point of use. A function calls the operations it needs, and any object that supplies them can work, regardless of its inheritance. This makes it easy to accept an existing or third-party type without adapting its class hierarchy.

For example, an application-owned set of payment strategies may benefit from a `PaymentMethod` ABC with a required `pay` method and shared validation. A utility that only needs `stream.read()` often works better with duck typing because files, in-memory buffers, and test doubles already provide that behaviour.

The trade-off is early enforcement versus flexibility. An ABC catches incomplete nominal implementations during instantiation, while plain duck typing may fail only when a missing operation is used. A static `Protocol` can document and check structural behaviour without requiring inheritance. The choice should match who owns the types and how strongly the runtime relationship matters.

sections.title: Nominal membership and structural capability answer different questions
sections.content:
A nominal model asks whether a type belongs to a declared family. Regular subclassing of an ABC makes that relationship visible in the MRO and lets the base enforce abstract members. This fits frameworks and domain models that own both the contract and most implementations.

A structural model asks whether the value can perform a particular job. An input object with `read` can be sufficient even if it was created by another library and knows nothing about the caller's abstractions. This keeps adapters and tests small, but the required operations must still be communicated.

Python also has middle ground. `typing.Protocol` supports structural checks by static tools. Some ABCs can register virtual subclasses or implement `__subclasshook__`, though registration does not add base methods to the registered class and does not place it in the MRO. These tools should clarify a real boundary rather than decorate every small function.

sections.title: Choose the contract style deliberately
sections.content:
| Concern | Abstract base class | Duck typing | Static `Protocol` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Declared inheritance required | Normally yes | No | No |
| Runtime instantiation check | Yes for unresolved abstract methods | No | No by itself |
| Accepts unrelated existing types | Only with adaptation or virtual registration | Yes | Yes when structure matches |
| Shared implementation | Can live in the base | Not implied | Not normally the purpose |
| Best fit | Owned runtime family | Small behaviour-based API | Documented structural typing |

sections.title: A duck-typed reader needs no shared base
sections.content:
```python
from io import StringIO

class FixedReader:
    def read(self):
        return "from custom reader"

def first_line(reader):
    return reader.read().splitlines()[0]

print(first_line(StringIO("from memory\nsecond line")))
print(first_line(FixedReader()))
```

Both objects work because they provide the one operation the function needs; neither inherits from an application-specific reader ABC.
